processing: Made as other Chinese black teas are: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried. A newer floral-fruity version adds a light tossing of the leaf after withering, borrowed from oolong work.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this tea specifically. As in other Chinese tea regions, spring leaf is the most valued; Hanzhong's northerly, cool climate makes its season relatively late.
appearance_dry: Typical of Chinese black teas of its kind: dark, fine twisted strips, sometimes with golden tips.
taste_profile: Few tasting accounts exist; expect the rounded sweetness of a northern Chinese black tea, and in the tossed style a more floral, fruity nose.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for fine Chinese black tea. Water a little off the boil keeps delicate leaf from turning sharp.

vintage_note: Like most Chinese black teas of this type it is normally sold as the current year's harvest, with spring lots priced highest. It is best drunk within a year or two; no ageing tradition is recorded for it.
description:
Hanzhong Hong is black tea from Hanzhong in southern Shaanxi, a place far better known for green tea, above all Hanzhong Xianhao. The city sits on the climate boundary between north and south China, which makes it one of the more northerly places to meet Chinese black tea.

The method is the familiar one of withering, rolling, oxidising and drying. A more recent variation tosses the withered leaf to bruise its edges, the step oolong makers use, and this is what gives the floral-fruity style its nose.

Little has been written about how it tastes as a class, so treat any promise on a label with some care. Fine Chinese black teas generally do well with short steeps and water just off the boil, and that is a sensible way to begin here.

Buy it as you would any regional black tea: ask for the harvest year and season, and which county it comes from. The name is used loosely for black tea from the area, not for one strictly defined recipe, so two bags can differ a lot.
history: Little is documented about when black tea making began in Hanzhong. The region's tea reputation rests on green tea, and its black tea looks like a later diversification. Work on a floral-fruity style was being published in the Chinese tea press by 2024.
